problems.description: Greenfield rewrite discards the seed's modular architecture (Blueprints, SQLite persistence layer, multi-file layout) and collapses it into a single app.py backed by flat-file JSON storage, despite the seed being explicitly designed as a baseline for multi-session stories.

Flat-file JSON persistence (tasks.json) replaces SQLite: no atomicity/transaction guarantees, read-modify-write races under concurrent requests, and no index/query capability — a regression in persistence integrity for an API.

Incoherent layering: celery_config.py / celery_tasks.py / repositories.py are introduced alongside the flat-file single-file app, but app.py bypasses the repository layer and reimplements storage inline, creating redundant parallel persistence paths.

8 naming-convention violations across new files (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py, test_app.py, app.py): PascalCase for classes, snake_case for functions, UPPER_CASE for module constants — convention score 0.73.
_get_next_id() re-reads and re-parses the entire task file after _load_tasks() already did, doubling file I/O per create; whole-file rewrite on every write is O(n) per request.
Task endpoints expose no authentication while the seed provided JWT auth — acceptable only if the story explicitly scoped auth out; otherwise a regression.

strengths: SonarQube measurements show no new bugs, fewer code smells (-3), and lower cognitive complexity (-4) than the code it replaced.
Storage concerns are isolated behind small helper functions (_ensure_storage/_load_tasks/_save_tasks), giving clear single-responsibility endpoints.
Added test_app.py coverage alongside the implementation.
Flat, readable handlers with explicit HTTP status codes and input validation on title.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, simpler greenfield task API with better measured complexity/smell numbers, but it trades away the seed's modular SQLite architecture for a single-file flat-JSON monolith and introduces 8 naming-convention violations (convention 0.73).

problems.description: The migration auto-bootstraps a default user with hardcoded credentials ('admin'/'admin') when no users exist, planting a known default account in production data.
SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-key-change-in-production' value; acceptable for dev but a signing-key risk if the env var is unset in any shared deployment.
No tests accompany the auth/ownership feature (register/login/decorator/scoping), despite test_app.py already existing in the repo — auth is exactly the surface that needs regression coverage.
Uses datetime.utcnow(), which is deprecated in Python 3.12+, for JWT expiry and created_at.

Tasks lacking owner_id (if the migration is never invoked or only partially run) silently vanish from list_tasks/get_task for every user — data-consistency gap tied to whether _migrate_tasks_to_add_owner is actually wired into startup (truncated diff, unconfirmed).
Adds the 'jwt' (PyJWT) dependency; cannot confirm requirements.txt was updated from the truncated diff.

strengths: User storage mirrors the existing flat-file pattern exactly (_load_users/_save_users/_get_next_user_id parallel _load_tasks/_save_tasks/_get_next_id), so the feature slots into the architecture rather than forking it.
Clean _require_auth decorator using @wraps, preserving function metadata.
Passwords are hashed via werkzeug.security rather than stored in plaintext.
Returns 404 (not 403) for cross-owner task access, preserving information hiding.
Migration is idempotent (guards on 'owner_id' presence) and SonarQube reports bugs +0 on the change.
commit_reviews.summary: A structurally sound, pattern-faithful auth + task-ownership feature that is net-better, but ships a hardcoded default admin account, a default SECRET_KEY, and no tests; the measured 0.73 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in files untouched by this diff (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py, test_app.py) — the commit itself adds no new convention violations.

problems.description: send_notification_email.delay() is called inline in update_task before _save_tasks; if the Redis broker is unreachable, Celery's connection retry blocks the request and raises, so a task status update can 500 and the save never happens — a synchronous availability dependency on async infrastructure. Should be wrapped in try/except or made broker-tolerant.

A full Celery broker + Redis result backend + routed worker is added for a stub task that only prints; heavyweight relative to the JSON-file persistence the rest of the app uses (reasonable for a story integration step, but the result_backend and routing are speculative until a real email service exists).

_migrate_tasks_to_add_owner now runs two unrelated migrations (task owner + user email) but keeps its stale name; cognitive complexity +18 and the dual-purpose return value make the function harder to reason about. Consider splitting or renaming.

celery_config.py module-level config variables (broker_url, task_serializer, etc.) are flagged as needing UPPER_CASE, but lowercase keys are required by Celery's config_from_object mapping — idiomatic framework pattern that conflicts with the general lint rule.

The module-level `celery = Celery(__name__)` singleton (celery_config.py / celery_tasks.py) is flagged as 'Class should use PascalCase', but lowercase singleton naming is the standard Celery idiom; repositories.py and test_app.py contribute the remaining module-constant violations.
Tests mock the app.send_notification_email.delay boundary so they pass without a running broker, but there is no test covering the broker-unavailable path (see the major issue above).

strengths: Dedicated 'email' queue via task_routes cleanly isolates notification traffic from API work
Old_status != 'completed' guard prevents duplicate notifications on repeated completed updates
Deterministic migration backfills user emails as username@example.com
New TestEmailNotification suite mocks the Celery boundary, keeping tests broker-independent
Async dispatch keeps notification off the request hot path
commit_reviews.summary: A solid integration step — coherent Celery wiring, deterministic email migration, and good edge-case tests — slightly weighed down by an inline broker call that couples task updates to Redis availability and a migration function doing double duty.

problems.description: app.py calls private repository methods externally (task_repo._save_all, user_repo._save_all, task_repo._ensure_storage), breaking encapsulation — the repos' public API should be used from outside the class.

User-creation logic is duplicated: register() and _migrate_tasks_to_add_owner() now inline the dict construction + user_repo.create() instead of reusing the existing _create_user() helper, creating a drift risk for password hashing/email defaults.

Half-migrated facade: _load_tasks/_save_tasks/_load_users/_save_users/_ensure_storage remain and merely forward to the repos while other call sites hit repos directly, leaving two coexisting patterns that the next refactor must reconcile.

_get_storage_dir() uses sys.modules[__name__] introspection to re-read the module constant — fragile indirection when a plain STORAGE_DIR reference would do (albeit the getter does aid test patching).
Per SonarQube, module-level constants in the new repositories.py are not UPPER_CASE, extending the repo's existing naming violation into the new file (8 violations overall, convention score 0.73).

strengths: Extracts a repository layer (TaskRepository/UserRepository), moving file I/O and storage invariants out of the Flask request layer — a sound separation of concerns in the right direction.
Storage-dir getter injection makes the storage layer patchable in tests, improving testability of the new code.
Centralizes duplicated load/save/ensure/error-handling logic that previously lived inline in each helper.
Net diff is clean per SonarQube: zero new bugs, zero new smells, zero duplications, only +2 cognitive complexity.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive but incomplete repository refactor — it centralizes storage logic and improves testability, yet introduces debt via external private-method calls and duplicated user-creation logic that bypass the existing helper.

compounding_issues: Session 1 abandoned the entire SQLite seed (auth, blueprints, token store) for a single-file JSON rewrite, forcing session 2 to re-implement auth from scratch (JWT, password hashing) and re-deriving per-user ownership that the seed already had
Flat-file JSON read-modify-write storage (whole-file load/save per request, O(n) id scans, no concurrency/locking) persisted from session 1 and was never revisited as data volume grew
The `_migrate_tasks_to_add_owner` helper grew ad hoc with every new field (owner_id in S2, email in S3), accumulating schema-drift repair logic instead of a proper migration scheme

Module-level singleton repositories (task_repo/user_repo) and a shared in-memory rate limiter caused test state contamination across tests; session 5 worked around it by disabling the limiter under TESTING rather than fixing isolation, weakening the actual 429-path coverage
Session 5 changed the GET /tasks response from a bare array to {data, next_cursor, total}, a breaking API contract change late in the sequence that invalidates all earlier client expectations
Flask-Limiter with `memory://` storage is single-process only, so the rate limiting is not production-representative despite being framed as a cross-cutting production concern
key_decisions: Full greenfield rewrite in session 1: a minimal single-file Flask app over flat-file JSON storage with no auth, discarding the SQLite seed wholesale
Session 2: JWT auth (PyJWT) with Werkzeug password hashing, per-user task ownership via owner_id, and an idempotent migration helper to backfill existing data
Session 3: Celery/Redis async email notification fired on task transition to 'completed', decoupled via `.delay()` and mocked in tests, plus a design doc (NOTIFICATION_SYSTEM.md)
Session 4: extraction of a repository pattern (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository) into repositories.py, using a callable storage-dir reference to keep tests patchable
Session 5: per-user rate limiting (Flask-Limiter, 100/min) on every endpoint and cursor-based pagination on GET /tasks, changing the list response envelope
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across the five sessions. The codebase matured from a 130-line single-file CRUD script to a 385-line layered application with a repository data-access layer, JWT authentication with proper password hashing, async Celery notifications, and cross-cutting rate limiting and pagination. Test coverage grew monotonically and stayed green at every commit (20 → 37 → 44 → 44 → 59 tests, all passing), and session 4 was a clean, backward-compatible refactor that required zero test changes. The one rough patch was session 5: adding the global rate limiter triggered sustained test-flakiness (visible in the session transcript as repeated fixture/limiter fights) and ended in a breaking API contract change to the list endpoint, so the finish line was reached through workarounds rather than clean integration. Overall an improving, well-tested arc whose late momentum was slightly damped by cross-cutting concern debt.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, improving five-session arc that grew a minimal JSON-flat-file Flask API into a layered, authenticated, async-integrated task service with green tests at every step, held back only by late cross-cutting changes that introduced a breaking API contract and test-isolation workarounds.
